newsitem.title: LAOS: Rare hearing on Lao dam opens amid controversy.
newsitem.headline: Rare hearing on Lao dam opens amid controversy.

text.p: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) largely stayed away on Monday from an unprecedented public discussion of a controversial Laos dam project, questioning the government's sincerity on hearing feedback.

NGO representatives said they doubted public opinion would actually be heeded on the the proposed $1.5 billion Nam Theun 2 dam project. The government is required by the World Bank to hold open discussions in return for partial loan guarantees.
The dam, which would be Laos' largest, is to be built on the Nakai Plateau, about 250 km east of Vientiane in central Laos.
NGO representatives also complained that only two weeks' notice was given for the meeting and that the format did not encourage open discussion.
Some called it a "public relations exercise".
Government officials said the meeting's start signalled the government's strong commitment to an open airing of the issue.

"This is the first public consultation that the Lao government has had," said Noulinh Sinbandhit, vice president of the government's Science Technology and Environment Organisation (STENO), which coordinated the meeting.
"We have to consult the population, especially the public sector, on this project," he told Reuters.
At least two NGOs were present -- the World Conservation Union and CARE International -- which are helping to study the effects of the proposed dam on the environment and local populations.
"The dam has really polarised people," said one international environmental worker.

The government says the build-operate-transfer (BOT) project will bring in $1 billion over 25 years, but will displace 1,000 families. It falls in a conservation zone and is believed to be located on a fault line, and could harm fisheries, critics say.

Finances are also being questioned. The government's power-purchase agreement with the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand expired when the dam ran into delays but project developers maintain the dam is economically viable.
The public nature of the issue is something new in this poor communist nation. "This is completely unprecedented," said one international observer.
The government has said hydroelectric power is indispensible for landlocked Laos, where per capita gross domestic product stands at just $350 per year.

The Lao government has asked the World Bank to provide partial loan guarantees for the project and has expressed hope that the International Finance Corporation would provide some equity in the project.
In turn, the World Bank has said Laos must hold several public consultations and carry out studies on the environmental, economic and social impact of the dam.

"We have been asked for a partial risk guarantee...which would provide commercial banks some comfort. But we have not yet taken any position on whether we should support this project or not," World Bank representative Kathryn McPhail told Reuters.

The World Bank's ultimate decision will be fateful for the project's five investors: Australia's Transfield Corp, Electricite de France, Thailand's Jasmine International, Italian-Thai Development Plc, and Thailand's Phatra Thanakit Plc.

"If the World Bank can't support the project, we will not proceed with being a part of it," said David Iverach, director of the consortium formed by the five companies, Nam Theung 2 Electricity Consortium.
